name: Language Change
miniText: The scientific question is whether speaker learning and social-network structure jointly change linguistic variants. In NetLogo's Language Change model, connected speakers produce utterances from competing grammars and alter their grammar use after hearing neighboring speakers. The selected literature connects this mechanism to network-mediated linguistic competition: utterance selection formalizes stochastic language-change mechanisms [1]; language competition offers a contrasting aggregate dynamics model [2]; degree-biased network growth contextualizes the models heterogeneous social connections [3]. Binary variants and simplified learning omit linguistic content and institutional prestige; language death is a related aggregate comparator, not this exact mechanism. The original NetLogo behavior is the baseline for reimplementation. This simulation offers a controlled thought experiment, and agreement with its output does not establish empirical validation.

verification.evidenceSummary: Systems as diverse as genetic networks or the World Wide Web are best described as networks with complex topology. A common property of many large networks is that the vertex connectivities follow a scale-free power-law distribution. This feature was found to be a consequence of two generic mechanisms: (i) networks expand continuously by the addition of new vertices, and (ii) new vertices attach preferentially to sites that are already well connected. A model based on these two ingredients reproduces the observed stationary scale-free distributions, which indicates that the development of large networks is governed by robust self-organizing phenomena that go beyond the particulars of the individual systems.
